newsitem.title: MAURITIUS: New Congo's mines minister sings for investors.
newsitem.headline: New Congo's mines minister sings for investors.

text.p: Kambale Mututulo is an unlikely government minister -- he loves jazz and sings for his supper. He is also a man with a very difficult job.

The new mines minister of the Democratic Republic of the Congo stunned hundreds of delegates to a recent sub-Saharan Oil and Minerals conference in Mauritius by starting his first speech to an international audience by breaking out in song.
"I have a dream," Mututulo sang, before urging international investors to put money into the former Zaire with its huge mineral potential in copper, cobalt, gold and diamonds.

Conference organisers said Mututulo, former head of the country's state business college who joined Laurent Kabila's forces after they launched their rebellion against Mobutu Sese Seko, loves jazz and even had his own band a few years ago.
Mututulo, a member of Kabila's inner circle and seen as very influential in the new government, was appointed mines minister after Kabila's troops captured the capital Kinshasa in May.
Now he has the unenviable task of overseeing rehabilitation of the mining industry in the new Congo -- once one of the biggest copper producers in the world and still the largest producer of cobalt.
Mining is in disarray after 32 years of rule by Mobutu's government, which siphoned millions of dollars from state mining companies into private pockets.
"At this most critical time when the Congo has finally been liberated...its industries are bankrupt and the need for a massive injection of investment has never been more urgent," Mututulo said.
Judging by the interest shown in his speech and later discussions at the Mauritius conference, the new Congo might just get the funds it needs to revive the mining industry.

Diamond giant De Beers Consolidated Mines Ltd. has changed its tune about the new mines minister who said he wanted to renegotiate De Beers' contract to buy diamonds from the Societe de Miniere de Bakwanga mine.
De Beers spokesman Tom Tweedy said Mututulo impressed South Africa's major mining houses at a recent meeting in Johannesburg.
"He had some quite nice things to say about De Beers. He was quite complimentary about De Beers," he said.
Already foreign firms like Tenke Mining Co., Barrick Gold Corp. and America Mineral Fields have sunk millions of dollars into the country.

Tenke is developing one of the largest copper projects in the world, in the south of the country. AMF won the rights to develop the Kolwezi copper/cobalt project in Katanga province, formerly Shaba -- the heart of the mining industry.
Dealing with scores of inquiries from potential investors seeking a stake in the country's vast mineral riches is not Mututulo's main concern.
The country's economy, on the verge of collapse after Mobutu's rule, is the major worry.
"Infrastructure and equipment necessary to maintain and increase economic production were allowed to deteriorate to the point of uselessness," Mututulo said.
"The state was the sole and major shareholder and thus castles in Shangri-la became more important than the basic necessities for our people," he said.
"This self-annointed neo-colonial African gentry took over most of the industries and proceeded to lead them straight to hell."

Mututulo said it was not easy to change the perceptions and habits of three decades under Mobutu and that many of the staff he inherited in the ministry were astounded at his long working hours -- much of the time fielding calls from potential investors.
